Cross-cultural studies, sometimes called holocultural studies or comparative studies, is a specialization in [anthropology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropology) and sister sciences such as [sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology), [psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology), [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics), [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science) that uses field data from many [societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society) through [comparative research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparative_research) to examine the scope of [human behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_behavior) and test hypotheses about human behavior and culture.

definition: cultural analysis is based on using [qualitative research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualitative_research) methods of the arts, [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities), [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_sciences), in particular [ethnography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnography) and [anthropology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropology), to collect data on [cultural phenomena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture) and to interpret cultural representations and practices; in an effort to gain new knowledge or understanding through analysis of that data and cultural processes.

Cultural anthropology is a branch of [anthropology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropology) focused on the study of [cultural variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_variation) among humans.

Cultural Anthropology is a quarterly [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed) [academic journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal) published by the [American Anthropological Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Anthropological_Association) on behalf of the [Society for Cultural Anthropology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_for_Cultural_Anthropology).

Cultural archive is a term associated with social [anthropologist Wendy James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_James_(anthropologist)) referencing the repository of knowledge found in everyday interactions that individuals reference to validate their existence in the world.
Cultural attractor theory focuses on how ideas being modified as they are transmitted between humans effects [cultural evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_evolution).
Cultural bias is the tendency of individuals to interpret and judge others' experiences through the lens of one's own cultural background.

Cultural competence, also known as intercultural competence, is a range of cognitive, [affective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affective), behavioral, and linguistic skills that lead to effective and appropriate [communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication) with people of other [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture)s.

Cultural consensus theory is an approach to information pooling or aggregation which supports a framework for the measurement and evaluation of beliefs as [cultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural); shared to some extent by a group of individuals.
Cultural determinism is the belief that the culture in which we are raised determines who we are at emotional and behavioral levels.

cultural diffusion is the spread of [cultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture) items—such as [idea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idea)s, [style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fashion)s, [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art), ] by Gail King and Meghan Wright, Anthropological Theories, M.D.
Cultural ecology is the study of human adaptations to social and physical environments.

Cultural group selection is an explanatory model within [cultural evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_evolution) of how cultural traits evolve according to the competitive advantage they bestow upon a group.
Cultural heritage management (CHM) is the vocation and practice of managing [cultural heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_heritage).

Cultural identity is a part of a person's [identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_(social_science)), or their self-conception and [self-perception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-perception), and is related to [nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationality), [ethnicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnicity), [religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion), [social class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_class), [generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation), [locality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality_(settlement)), [gender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender), or any kind of social group that has its own distinct [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture).

Cultural layer is a key concept in [archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology), particularly [culture-historical archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture-historical_archaeology) especially in [archaeological digs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological_excavation) or excavations.

Cultural loss refers to the erosion, disappearance, or transformation of the practices, languages, identities, knowledge systems, beliefs, arts, and social structures that define a community or society.

Cultural materialism is an [anthropological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropology) research orientation first introduced by [Marvin Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Harris) in his 1968 book The Rise of Anthropological Theory, ==See also== *[Marvin Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Harris) *[Maxine Margolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxine_Margolis) *[[Jerald T.

Cultural practice is the manifestation of a [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture) or [sub-culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-culture), especially in regard to the traditional and customary practices of a particular [ethnic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnicity) or other cultural group.

Cultural relativism is the view that the [values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_(ethics)) (such as moral values) of a [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture) must be understood in their own cultural context and not judged according to the standards of a different culture.

cultural resource management (CRM) is the practice of managing cultural resources —What the Maritime Heritage Crisis Says About Archaeology, Cultural Resource Management, and Global Ecological Breakdown.

Cultural Survival is an Indigenous-led [nonprofit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization) [(501(c)(3))](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/501(c)(3)_organization), based in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts), United States, that advocates for the rights of [Indigenous Peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples) around the world.
cultural system is the interaction of different elements in [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture).
cultural trait is a single identifiable material or non-material element within a [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture), and is conceivable as an object in itself.

culture of capitalism or capitalist culture is the set of social practices, [social norms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_norms), values and patterns of behavior that are attributed to the capitalist economic system in a capitalist society.

culture of poverty is a concept in [social theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_theory) that asserts that the [values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_(ethics)) of people experiencing poverty play a significant role in perpetuating their impoverished condition, sustaining a [cycle of poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_of_poverty) across generations.

Culture shock is an experience a person may have when moving to a cultural environment which is different from one's own; it is also the personal disorientation a person may feel when experiencing an unfamiliar way of life due to [immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration) or a visit to a new country, a move between social environments, or simply transition to another type of life.

culture-bound syndrome, culture-specific syndrome, or folk illness is a combination of psychiatric and somatic [symptom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symptom)s that are considered to be a recognizable disease only within a specific society or [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture).

media.file: Stony Stratford Ridge This shape survives in some places as curved field boundaries, even where the ridge and furrow pattern itself has vanished. If the oxen had been turned right at the end of the furrow, they would immediately have had to turn right again down the returning furrow, making the line of oxen cut across the top of the ploughed strip and thus pulling the plough out of the ground before it reached the end of the furrow, as well as having potential difficulty from two adjacent lines of oxen moving in opposite directions. Alternatively, if lined up rightwards along the headland, some would already be past the beginning of the new furrow, and these would have to be moved awkwardly sideways into the furrow to be ready to plough. Turning to the left made one turn at a time and avoided a sideways move. As oxen became larger and ploughs more efficient, smaller teams were needed. Zgërdhesh is an [archeological site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archeological_site) in [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania).

Zooarchaeology by mass spectrometry, commonly referred to by the abbreviation ZooMS, is a scientific method that identifies animal species by means of characteristic [peptide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peptide) sequences in the [protein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein) [collagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collagen).

Umq al-Rabach (or ʿUmq al-Rabaḫ), al-Sharqiyah, [Sultanate of Oman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultanate_of_Oman) is an archaeological site of the [Samad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samad) [Late Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Iron_Age) and [Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic) Periods.
